newsitem.title: USA: U.S hits report it could live with separate Quebec.
newsitem.headline: U.S hits report it could live with separate Quebec.

text.p: The United States on Thursday disavowed an article written by one of its diplomats saying that Washington "could live" with a separate Quebec, and it reaffirmed support for a "strong, united Canada."

"Nobody -- no diplomat serving in the United States government has the right to, in effect, stand up in a theatre and yell 'fire,' and this is the diplomatic equivalent of it," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said of an article written by David Jones, a former political officer at the U.S. embassy in Ottawa but now in a different capacity.
The controversial article was published in the spring magazine of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Jones from 1992-96 was a political officer at the American Embassy in Ottawa.
He describes Canada's French-speaking province of Quebec as a mature, sophisticated and modern society that is capable of surviving on its own without suffering traumatic consequences.

"Quebec would not be a Mozambique, Chad, Bolivia, Nepal or some other developing world basket case," Jones writes. "It does not take much examination to recognise that Quebec qualifies as a nation-state."
Jones also wrote: "Although it is clear that a united Canada is in the U.S. interest, it is equally clear that the United States could live with a disunited Canada."

He said Quebec was not a security threat, would maintain a commitment to free trade, has a solid economy, is democratic and the prospects for violence should the province declare independence from the rest of Canada are "overblown."
Burns, at the State Department daily news briefing, said Jones had not cleared the article with him as required and called this breach "an outrageous act, an undisciplined act."

"If Jones's article had been on my desk, if he'd had the decency to give that article to me and my bureau to clear it, I would not have cleared it, because it does not represent the views of our government," Burns said.

"He does not have a right to publish his private views and not check with us first because, the last time I checked, we're paying him. He's still on the rolls of the U.S. government, even though he's left Embassy Ottawa," Burns added.
The spokesman indicated Jones had had a "political argument" with his superiors over the Quebec issue and stressed that the views in the article are Jones' alone.

He said Jones is no longer advising President Bill Clinton and the secretary of state on Canadian matters but working in the State Department's Freedom of Information office, which processes requests for government information.
Burns repeated the U.S.'s position on Quebec separation is one of believing in "a strong and united Canada."
A referendum on the separation of Quebec from Canada was narrowly defeated in October, 1995 and supporters of Quebec independence have vowed to try again to break the province away Canada.
